name: Priya Novak

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Priya. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to tech companies, employers, unions or government. Nothing you say will carry your name, so you're free to tell me the public version and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's two jobs, really. Mornings I'm out on the farm, which is my Uncle Marek's: a bit of everything, 80 ewes, some barley, potatoes, and 500 free-range hens. Then from about eleven I'm in the farm shop we run by the road, serving, doing the meat counter with my aunt, and doing all the online side, the orders and the posts. I'm still the junior, Uncle Marek reminds me of that daily.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the shop on a Saturday when it's busy and people ask where the lamb came from and I can point out the window. What wears me out is that I'm doing two jobs on one low wage, and I've got maybe two weeks of money saved. I use AI every day for the shop: writing posts, planning stock, answering emails. My partner Daniel teaches at the primary school, and we rent a small house in the village.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ha. I'd still use it for the posts. It writes a better product description than I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a useful tool and people got carried away. At the shop I'd tell customers nothing's changed, the eggs are still from our hens. Online I'd probably make a joke post about it, it'd get good engagement.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it'd be fine for me, because the shop's what keeps the farm alive, and that would carry on. The worry would be the usual stuff: the supermarket opening a big store on the bypass, and Uncle Marek refusing to put the prices up. AI flopping doesn't sell more lamb.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going, use the AI for the shop like I do now, and push to start online delivery to the town, maybe £5 a drop. I'd want to start a little side thing, farm visits for school groups, which Daniel could help me set up. And I'd talk Uncle Marek into a card machine at the egg stall, because people don't carry cash.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A bit restless, though. I always want to be doing the next thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the shop keeps the farm alive. How so?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd lose money on the lamb if we sold it at the market. In the shop we sell it as chops and mince with our name on, and we get double. Without the shop, Uncle Marek would have sold up years ago.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does your family feel about your ideas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My aunt loves them, my uncle grumbles and then does half of them. That's how it works in our family. You respect the older ones, but you keep pushing, politely.

S0.say: I'd say AI is a useful tool and people got carried away. I'd tell customers nothing's changed, the eggs are still from our hens, and make a joke post that would do well.
S0.think: It'd be fine for me, because the shop keeps the farm alive and that would carry on. The worry is the usual stuff: a supermarket on the bypass and my uncle refusing to put prices up.
S0.do: Keeps using AI daily for the shop and pushes to start online delivery to the town at about £5 a drop. Sets up farm visits for school groups as a side business with her partner's help.
S0.feel: Calm but restless, always wanting to do the next thing.
S0.quote: My aunt loves them, my uncle grumbles and then does half of them.
S0.fieldNote: Priya is a natural seller and the most commercially minded person in this group, using AI daily to run the shop side. She speaks warmly of family hierarchy while pushing change politely. Her worries are about competition and pricing, not AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Steady change. Honestly, I think that's good for us. Small farms that sell direct.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's an opportunity for family farms, if we're smart. At the shop I'd lean into the human side: real people, real animals, you can meet the farmer. Online I'd post about it as a selling point.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the big farms go full robot and their food gets cheaper and more boring. That's good for us, because some people will always pay for a story and a face. But I'd also want robots on our side, doing the dull jobs, so we can spend more time in the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd talk Uncle Marek into a robot egg collector for the hen house, maybe on a lease so it doesn't cost us everything up front. I'd start the delivery round and the school visits. And I'd ask Daniel to help write a little website that explains how we farm, so it's not just pictures.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Excited. Like the first warm day in spring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said real people is a selling point. Isn't it odd to use robots behind the scenes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a little. But people don't mind a milking machine, they mind not knowing who you are. If the robot collects eggs and I spend that hour talking to customers, that's a better farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your uncle say about the robot?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say his father never needed one. Then he'd watch the neighbour's for a month and ask me how much. He's not against new things, he's against wasting money.

S1.say: It's an opportunity for family farms if we're smart. I'd lean into the human side at the shop, real people and real animals, and post about it online as a selling point.
S1.think: The big farms will go full robot and their food gets cheaper and more boring, which helps us because some people will always pay for a story and a face. But I'd want robots doing our dull jobs too.
S1.do: Persuades her uncle to lease a robot egg collector rather than buy it outright. Starts the delivery round and school visits, and builds a website with her partner explaining how they farm.
S1.feel: Excited, like the first warm day in spring.
S1.quote: People don't mind a milking machine, they mind not knowing who you are.
S1.fieldNote: Priya sees Steady Disruption as a chance for family farms that sell direct, and she's happy to use robots behind the scenes to free up time with customers. She handled the gentle contradiction well. Her uncle's caution about money, not technology, shapes what she can do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Okay. That's a different thing entirely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say small family businesses are what will hold towns together, so support your local farm shop. I'd be pushing that at the shop and online. I wouldn't be blaming anyone, just getting on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the shop could survive, but its customers might not. If half the village is out of work, who's buying £8 sausages? That's the bit that scares me. The robots don't bother me, the empty tills do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the first month I'd get Uncle Marek to put robots on the routine jobs, the hens and the potatoes, so the farm costs less to run. I'd drop the prices on the basics and keep the posh stuff for weekends. I'd turn the shop into a place people come to, a café corner, so it's a bit of the village that still has people in it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. More about the village than about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your uncle. Would he agree to robots that fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not easily. He'd fight me. But if I showed him the numbers, that it's robots or selling up, he'd do it. He loves the farm more than he hates gadgets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With two weeks of savings, how would you and Daniel get by?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Daniel's teaching might go too, the card says almost any work. So we'd cut right back, move into the flat above the shop, and live off the business. Family helps family. That's how we'd do it.

S2.say: Small family businesses are what will hold towns together, so support your local farm shop. I'd push that at the shop and online, and just get on with it without blaming anyone.
S2.think: The shop could survive, but its customers might not. If half the village is out of work, who's buying £8 sausages? The robots don't bother me, the empty tills do.
S2.do: Gets her uncle to put robots on routine jobs within a month, cuts prices on basics and adds a café corner to the shop. Moves with her partner into the flat above the shop to live off the family business.
S2.feel: Anxious, more for the village than for herself.
S2.quote: The robots don't bother me, the empty tills do.
S2.fieldNote: Priya's insight is that a fast change threatens her customers more than her work. She responds by cutting costs with robots and making the shop a community place. Her answer to money trouble is family, not government, which fits her outlook.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. I can work with five years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is time for small businesses to get ready, and the government should get out of the way and let us. At the shop and online I'd keep pushing local food and local jobs. I'd tell other farm shops to team up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years is a good run for us. I could build the delivery round and the visits, get robots on the dull jobs, and maybe buy into the farm properly. The risk is the same as before: if nobody has wages, nobody buys.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In year one I'd lease the egg robot, start delivery and the school visits. By year two I'd want a proper website and a group of five or six farm shops sharing one delivery van. And I'd ask Uncle Marek about buying a share of the business, slowly, out of my wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly excited. I like a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five or six farm shops sharing a van. Who'd organise that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Me, probably, with AI doing the routes. I know three of the other shops already from the farmers' market. Nobody else has time, and I don't mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Buying a share on a low wage. How realistic is that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Slowly. A few hundred pounds a year at first, as Uncle Marek wants. It's family, so it's not about the price, it's about him trusting me to keep it going. That's worth more than money.

S3.say: Five years is time for small businesses to get ready, and the government should get out of the way and let us. I'd keep pushing local food and local jobs and tell other farm shops to team up.
S3.think: Five years is a good run: delivery, visits, robots on dull jobs and maybe a proper share of the farm. The risk is the same: if nobody has wages, nobody buys.
S3.do: Leases the egg robot and starts delivery and school visits in year one. By year two builds a shared delivery van with five or six farm shops and begins buying a small share of her uncle's business.
S3.feel: Uneasy but mostly excited; she likes a plan.
S3.quote: It's family, so it's not about the price, it's about him trusting me to keep it going.
S3.fieldNote: With five years Priya builds outward, organising other farm shops and using AI for routes. Buying into the family business is about trust as much as money for her. She keeps returning to the same risk: customers without wages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's long enough to really build something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty of time for families and small businesses to get ready. I'd tell young people to learn the tools and start something. Online I'd be sharing what we're doing, as an example.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, ten years could make me. I could own part of the farm, run the shop, maybe open a second one. But I'd be 37 and I'd want kids by then, and I'd want to know there's still a village for them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First two years: delivery, visits, the egg robot, saving where I can. By year five, a share in the farm and maybe a second shop in town. By year eight, robots on most of the field work so the family can focus on the shop and the visits. And Daniel and I would plan for kids around year four.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm and hopeful. Like a good harvest coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would a village need to stay alive in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somewhere to go and someone to talk to. The church, the school, the shop. If those stay, people stay. I'd want the shop to be one of them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to someone your age who's frightened by all this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Don't sit and wait for someone to save you. Learn the tools, work with your family, and start something small. That's not me being hard. It's what my grandmother did when she came here with nothing.

S4.say: Ten years is plenty of time for families and small businesses to get ready. I'd tell young people to learn the tools and start something, and share what we're doing online as an example.
S4.think: Ten years could make me: part of the farm, the shop, maybe a second one. But I'd be 37, I'd want kids, and I'd want to know there's still a village for them.
S4.do: Builds delivery, visits and the egg robot in the first two years, then buys a share of the farm and opens a second shop by year five. Plans children with her partner around year four and automates most field work by year eight.
S4.feel: Calm and hopeful, like a good harvest coming in.
S4.quote: Don't sit and wait for someone to save you. Learn the tools, work with your family, and start something small.
S4.fieldNote: Ten years turns Priya's ideas into a full business plan, ending with robots in the fields and family in the shop. She links her drive to her grandmother arriving with nothing. Her picture of a living village, church, school and shop, shows her traditional values alongside her ease with technology.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. Not for the farm so much, we'd adapt, but for the village. If people lose their wages that fast, nobody can afford to buy from us, and the place goes quiet. What would help is lower taxes and less red tape for small family businesses, and something that keeps money in people's pockets so towns don't empty out.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who we'd sell to. Everybody asks about jobs. Nobody asks who's still got money to spend when the jobs go.

headlineQuote: The robots don't bother me, the empty tills do.
portrait: Priya Novak is a 27-year-old junior on her uncle's mixed family farm, splitting her day between the fields and the farm shop, where she uses AI every day for posts, stock and orders. She lives with her partner Daniel, a primary school teacher, and has about two weeks of savings. She is a natural seller who respects the family hierarchy while politely pushing change. Across the pictures she happily puts robots on the dull jobs and leans into the human face of the shop. Her deepest fear in AGI by 2028 is not robots but a village of customers with no wages, and with more time she plans to buy into the farm, open a second shop and start a family.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because if people lose their wages that fast, nobody can afford to buy from the shop and the village goes quiet.
whatWouldHelp: Lower taxes and less red tape for small family businesses, and something that keeps money in people's pockets so towns don't empty out.
